834.title: Call me bitter (Ruth 1:1–21)
834.hook: Naomi loses husband and sons in Moab and asks to be called Mara, bitter
834.carry: stay beside them, let their words stand
834.tomorrow: Thy people shall be my people (Ruth 1:16–17)
834.howItsDone: The book of Ruth is read in synagogue on Shavuot, and Jews count it among the short scrolls of the Writings.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Ketuvim, the Writings, opened in human voices. Your line was they praise, they doubt, they complain. Today, the first story on the Talmud's list.

Two women walk into Bethlehem, dusty from the road, and the whole town comes out to look. In the King James, "all the city was moved about them, and they said, Is this Naomi?" She left with a husband and two sons. She's come back with none of them, and the woman beside her is a foreigner from Moab. The neighbors aren't cruel. They're just shocked; they can barely match the face they knew to the one in front of them. And Naomi answers in a way nobody expects. She tells them to stop using her name.
screen: `TWO WOMEN WALK INTO BETHLEHEM.` → `IS THIS NAOMI?` → `STOP USING MY NAME.`

segments.voice: Go back to how the book begins: "in the days when the judges ruled," a famine in the land. A man of Bethlehem, Elimelech, takes his wife Naomi and their two sons to the fields of Moab to survive. There Elimelech dies. The sons marry Moabite women, Orpah and Ruth. Then both sons die. The King James puts it in one bare line: "the woman was left of her two sons and her husband." Left. That's the word for her. When she hears there's bread again at home, she sets out, and on the road she begs her daughters-in-law to go back to their mothers. Orpah, weeping, goes. Ruth won't. That moment is tomorrow's. Today belongs to Naomi at the city gate. "Call me not Naomi, call me Mara: for the Almighty hath dealt very bitterly with me." Mara means bitter. Then: "I went out full, and the LORD hath brought me home again empty." Notice three things. First, she says it out loud, in public, and she says it about God; she doesn't pretend to be fine for the neighbors. Second, the book doesn't correct her. No one tells her to look on the bright side, and her words are kept, exactly as she said them, in Scripture. Third, the quiet ache: when Naomi says empty, Ruth is standing right next to her, the one person who stayed. Grief that deep can't see it yet, and the story doesn't rush her. It only adds that they arrived at the beginning of barley harvest.

If you pray, you can hold them before God without words.

835.title: Thy people shall be my people (Ruth 1:16–17)
835.hook: Ruth clings to Naomi: "thy people shall be my people, and thy God my God"
835.howItsDone: Jews read Ruth's vow in the book of Ruth on Shavuot, and Jewish tradition looks to Ruth as the example of someone who joins the Jewish people by choice.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Naomi asked to be called Mara. Your line was stay beside them, let their words stand. Today, back on the road, to hear Ruth.
screen: `STAY BESIDE THEM, LET THEIR WORDS STAND.`

segments.voice: On the road out of Moab, Naomi keeps sending her daughters-in-law home, and her argument is practical, almost brutal. I'm too old to have a husband. Even if I had sons tonight, would you wait for them to grow up? Go back. Orpah weeps, kisses her, and turns for home, and the book never blames her. Ruth doesn't move. So Naomi points after her. In the King James: "Behold, thy sister in law is gone back unto her people, and unto her gods: return thou after thy sister in law." It's the last door Naomi can open for her. And Ruth closes it.
screen: `GO BACK, I HAVE NOTHING TO GIVE.` → `ORPAH TURNS FOR HOME.` → `RETURN THOU AFTER THY SISTER.`

segments.voice: Ruth's answer holds today's title: "thy people shall be my people, and thy God my God." Listen to how it ends. "Where thou diest, will I die, and there will I be buried: the LORD do so to me, and more also, if ought but death part thee and me." Three things are packed in. First, she goes past a lifetime: not just I'll come with you, but I'll be buried where you're buried. Not even her bones are going back to Moab. Second, she seals it with an oath by the LORD, the name of Naomi's God: a woman of Moab, on a road out of Moab, binding herself in the name she's choosing. Third, look at Naomi. "When she saw that she was stedfastly minded to go with her, then she left speaking unto her." That's all. No embrace in the text. No thank you. Naomi just stops arguing, they walk on, and the next thing she says out loud, at the gate, is that she came home empty. Ruth's loyalty isn't thanked on the spot. It doesn't need to be. The rabbis heard more. In the Talmud, in tractate Yevamot, they imagine a whole conversation hidden in the speech: Naomi naming, one by one, what this life will ask of her, and each of Ruth's phrases answering, I accept. And some readers find one word under all of it, a word Ruth never says but lives out: chesed, loyal kindness that keeps going after it's been told to stop.

836.title: Some handfuls (Ruth 2)
836.hook: Boaz tells his workers to "let fall also some of the handfuls" for her
836.howItsDone: Jewish teaching on giving, rooted in the laws of leaving gleanings and the corners of the field, prizes gifts that protect the dignity of the one who receives, and the book of Ruth is read in synagogue on Shavuot.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Ruth's vow, and the chesed she never named. Your line was thy people, my people. Today, the two women are home and need to eat.

The King James says it just happened: "her hap was to light on a part of the field belonging unto Boaz." Ruth goes out to glean, to pick up the stalks the reapers drop, which the Torah leaves for the poor and the stranger. She wanders into one field among many. The owner walks out from Bethlehem right then and greets his workers: "The LORD be with you." They call back: "The LORD bless thee." A boss and his reapers, blessing each other in the barley. Then he notices the stranger.
screen: `HER HAP WAS TO LIGHT ON THIS FIELD.` → `THE LORD BE WITH YOU.` → `HE NOTICES THE STRANGER.`

segments.voice: Boaz asks who she is, and hears: the Moabite girl who came back with Naomi. So he tells her: stay in my field, drink from the water my young men draw, I've told them not to touch you. Ruth falls on her face. "Why have I found grace in thine eyes, that thou shouldest take knowledge of me, seeing I am a stranger?" His answer: I've heard everything you did for your mother-in-law, how you left your father and mother and the land you were born in. And he blesses her by the God "under whose wings thou art come to trust." At mealtime he hands her roasted grain; she eats her fill and has some left over, which she saves for Naomi. Then the line in today's title. When Ruth gets up to glean again, Boaz orders his reapers: "let fall also some of the handfuls of purpose for her, and leave them, that she may glean them, and rebuke her not." No sack handed over in front of everyone. He has the extra dropped on purpose where she'll find it, so it looks like ordinary gleaning, and she gathers it with her own hands. Rebuke her not: nobody stands over her. The gift is real, and her dignity stays whole. That evening she carries home so much barley that Naomi asks where she worked. Ruth says the name: Boaz. And the woman who came home empty says: "Blessed be he of the LORD, who hath not left off his kindness to the living and to the dead." Mara is blessing someone again.

837.title: From outsider to ancestor (Ruth 4)
837.hook: the Moabite woman becomes the great-grandmother of King David
837.tomorrow: A man in the land of Uz
837.howItsDone: Jewish communities read the book of Ruth on the festival of Shavuot, and Ruth is remembered in Jewish tradition as a woman who chose to join the Jewish people and as an ancestor of King David.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Boaz had extra grain dropped for Ruth to glean. Your line was let fall some handfuls. Today, the last chapter of Ruth.

The book of Ruth ends with a list of names. First, a morning at the city gate, where a town did its business. Boaz sits down there, calls over a nearer kinsman of Naomi's, and gathers elders of the city as witnesses. Naomi is selling a piece of land, he says, and you have the first right to buy it back. Sure, says the man, I'll redeem it. Then the rest: the land comes with Ruth, the Moabite widow, and with keeping her late husband's name alive. The man backs out. He pulls off his shoe and hands it over, the old way of sealing a deal, and the field and the future pass to Boaz.
screen: `A MORNING AT THE CITY GATE.` → `THE NEARER KINSMAN BACKS OUT.` → `A SHOE SEALS THE DEAL.`

segments.voice: Notice what the book keeps calling her, right to the end: not Ruth the wife of Boaz, but Ruth the Moabitess. In chapter two she called herself a foreigner, and the story never pretends otherwise. She marries Boaz, and a son is born. Then the camera swings to Naomi, who came home empty and asked to be called bitter. The women of Bethlehem praise Ruth to her face, in the King James words: "thy daughter in law, which loveth thee, which is better to thee than seven sons." Seven sons, said to a woman who buried two. Naomi lays the baby in her lap and cares for him, and the neighbors name him: "There is a son born to Naomi; and they called his name Obed: he is the father of Jesse, the father of David." David. His great-grandmother came from Moab, a people the Torah elsewhere keeps out of the assembly. The rabbis noticed. The Talmud records a reading that the old rule names Moabite men, not Moabite women, which left a door open for Ruth. The book just ends with the family line, and the last name on it is David. Tradition reads Ruth on Shavuot, the festival of receiving the Torah, and some readers hear why: Ruth chose to come in. A story that began with a famine and three graves ends with a cradle and a king. She never stopped being an outsider. She became an ancestor anyway.

838.title: A man in the land of Uz (Job 1:1–12)
838.hook: a blameless man, and the adversary's question: does he serve for nothing?
838.howItsDone: Job is one of the books of the Writings, the third part of the Tanakh. Jews study it as a book of wisdom and argument about suffering, and traditional study includes the rabbis' debate over whether Job was a real man or a parable.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Ruth the Moabitess became King David's great-grandmother. Your line was a cradle and a king. Today, a new book in the Writings: Job.

"There was a man in the land of Uz, whose name was Job." It opens like a bedtime story: no king's name, no year, no map. The book never says where Uz is. The man is perfect and upright, the text says, one who feared God and turned away from evil. He has sons and daughters, flocks and herds. His children take turns throwing feasts in each other's homes, and after every round Job rises early to offer sacrifices for them, in case one of them sinned and cursed God in their heart. A careful father with nothing to hide. Then the scene changes, and we're not in Uz anymore.
screen: `A MAN IN THE LAND OF UZ.` → `PERFECT AND UPRIGHT.` → `UP EARLY FOR HIS CHILDREN.`

segments.voice: We're in heaven, at a gathering before God, and one who comes is called, in Hebrew, ha-satan. The word has "the" in front of it: the adversary, the accuser. He isn't a ruler of his own kingdom here. He comes with the others and answers to God. God speaks first: "Hast thou considered my servant Job, that there is none like him in the earth?" And the adversary asks the question the whole book lives inside: "Doth Job fear God for nought?" Look at the fence you've put around him, his house, his work, his flocks. Take it away, and he'll curse you to your face. God allows it: everything Job has is in your hand, but don't touch the man himself. Job knows none of this. That's the strange gift of the book: we know why it's happening, and Job never does. Some readers hear the question turned on themselves. Is goodness a deal? Am I kind because it works, honest because it pays, faithful because life has gone well? Or is there something underneath that would stay if the rewards stopped? The rabbis didn't agree on who Job was. In the Talmud, one teacher says Job never lived at all, that the book is a parable, and others argue for different ages and places. Either way, Uz could be anywhere, and the man could be anyone.
screen: `HA-SATAN: THE ADVERSARY.` · `DOTH JOB FEAR GOD FOR NOUGHT?` · `WE KNOW WHY. JOB NEVER DOES.` · `A REAL MAN, OR A PARABLE?`

segments.voice: Pick one good thing you do, calling your mother, honest work, giving, praying, patience with a kid, and ask it quietly: would I still do this if nothing came back? Don't answer, and don't decide you're a fraud or a saint; let the question sit, unanswered, the way it sits at the start of this book. If you pray, you can bring the question to God as it is.

839.title: Gave and taken (Job 1:20–22)
839.hook: "the LORD gave, and the LORD hath taken away"
839.carry: naked came I out of my mother's womb
839.howItsDone: Jewish mourners tear a garment, called keriah, when they learn of a close relative's death, and Job's words, the LORD gave and the LORD has taken away, are part of the traditional Jewish burial service.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the adversary asked whether Job fears God for nothing. Your line was is it for nothing. Today, the question gets its first answer.

A messenger runs up to Job. Raiders came and took the oxen and the donkeys and killed the servants, "and I only am escaped alone to tell thee." While he's still speaking, a second: fire fell from the sky and burned up the sheep. While he's still speaking, a third: raiders took the camels. While he's still speaking, a fourth. Your sons and daughters were eating together in their oldest brother's house, and a great wind came from the wilderness and struck the four corners of the house, and it fell on them. They're dead. The text gives no pause between the messengers. It all lands at once.
screen: `WHILE HE WAS YET SPEAKING.` → `ONE MESSENGER, THEN ANOTHER.` → `THE HOUSE FALLS.`

segments.voice: Watch what Job does, in order. "Then Job arose, and rent his mantle, and shaved his head, and fell down upon the ground, and worshipped." Grief comes first, and it's physical, and the book doesn't hurry him past it. Jewish mourners still tear a garment at a death; the tearing is called keriah. Only then, from the ground, Job speaks: "Naked came I out of my mother's womb, and naked shall I return thither: the LORD gave, and the LORD hath taken away; blessed be the name of the LORD." Everything I had was given; none of it was mine to keep. And still, from the floor, a blessing. Not instead of grief, but in the middle of it, with the robe already torn. The narrator adds one line: "In all this Job sinned not, nor charged God foolishly." The adversary said Job would curse God to his face. He doesn't. Tradition put Job's words into the Jewish burial service, so mourners say this line at the graveside. Some find it a comfort; some find it almost impossible to say. Both are honest, and the book has room for both, because this isn't Job's last word. He'll have much more to say, and not all of it gentle. Today, this is where he kneels.

840.title: Seven silent days (Job 2:11–13)
840.hook: Job's friends sit with him seven days without a word, the best thing they do
840.howItsDone: During shiva, the week of mourning, Jewish mourners stay at home and visitors come to comfort them; by tradition visitors wait for the mourner to speak first, a custom the Talmud ties to Job's friends.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Job tore his robe and said, the LORD gave and the LORD hath taken away. Your line was naked came I out of my mother's womb. This week ran from Naomi's bitterness, through Ruth's promise and the handfuls in the field, to King David's family line and the land of Uz. It ends in silence.
screen: `NAKED CAME I OUT OF MY MOTHER'S WOMB.`

segments.voice: It gets worse. In chapter two the adversary comes back, and this time Job's own body is struck, with sore boils from the sole of his foot to the top of his head. He sits among the ashes, scraping his skin with a broken piece of pottery. His wife tells him to curse God and die. He answers: "shall we receive good at the hand of God, and shall we not receive evil?" Far off, three friends hear the news: Eliphaz, Bildad and Zophar. They arrange to meet, and they travel to Job together, to mourn with him and comfort him.
screen: `BOILS, ASHES, A BROKEN POT.` → `SHALL WE NOT RECEIVE EVIL?` → `THREE FRIENDS SET OUT.`

segments.voice: From a distance, they don't recognize him. They weep out loud, tear their robes, and throw dust into the air so it falls on their heads. Then the line this day is named for: "So they sat down with him upon the ground seven days and seven nights, and none spake a word unto him: for they saw that his grief was very great." On the ground, in the ashes, at his level. And none of them spoke, because they saw: this grief was bigger than anything they could say. Some readers call this the best thing the friends do in the whole book. Hold on to that, because soon they'll start talking. The rabbis learned something practical here. The Talmud teaches that people who come to comfort a mourner shouldn't speak until the mourner speaks first, and it draws that rule from Job: his friends waited, and Job opened his mouth. Jewish mourning still has a week of sitting, called shiva, when the family stays home and visitors come to them. The custom is to come in, sit down, and let the mourner lead. It's a hard skill. When someone is hurting, the urge to fill the air is strong: an explanation, a story, a bright side. For seven days, the friends resisted it. They brought only themselves.
